newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian sugar industry sees little hope from budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian sugar industry sees little hope from budget.

text.p: The Indian sugar industry, bulging with stocks, has asked the government to slap tariffs on sugar imports but expects few sops from the federal budget, industry officials said on Monday.
"On the sugar industry, I am not expecting anything particular, it is not a budget-linked industry," Shanti Lal Jain, director general of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) told Reuters.
Jain said the sugar industry had demanded that in view of high domestic sugar stocks the government in its federal budget should levy a 30 percent duty on sugar imports.

India allowed free sugar exports to augment stocks after production fell two years ago. Sugar output has since picked up but government has continued with the policy on free imports to keep prices under check.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to present the 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament on February 28.

Analysts said sugar was a highly politicised commodity in India and a package of measures was needed to get the best from the industry. Sugar supplies and pricing in India are controlled by the government.
The mills supply 40 percent of their output as levy sugar at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor, and sell the rest in the open market.
Industry officials say their losses are growing because there is a gap of nearly 40 percent between open market sugar prices and the price it has to sell subsidised sugar at.

India began abolishing licences for many industries under a reform programme that began in 1991, but it kept sugar under the old regime, which has subsidised prices for consumers and protected producers.
"I don't expect anything so far as sugar is concerned because no politician understands or tries to understand the industry," said Indhubhai Patel, a senior industry official.
"We have made a strong plea to the government for 30 percent import duty on sugar," Jain said. "There is no justification for continuing free imports."
Jain said the cost of producing sugar for domestic consumption and sale was higher than sugar set aside for exports because of government controls.
Industry officials say they were exporting essentially to liquidate stocks and cut down their overheads.
"India might become a dumping ground for sugar. It could happen," Jain said.
In January India decided to end the export monopoly of the Indian Sugar and General Industries Import-Export Corp (ISGIEC), a body set up by private millers.

India produced an all-time high of 16.4 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 (October-September) and the new season started with stocks as high as 8.1 million tonnes, government officials said. Output for 1996/97 is forecast at 14 million tonnes.
"Even if 1996/97 production is lower than last year, we may still begin next year with a surplus of 7.5-8.0 million tonnes," Jain said. India annually consumes about 13 million tonnes of sugar.
India exported a little more than one million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96. The government has authorised the export of 250,000 tonnes of sugar in the 1996/97 sugar season.
"It is high time the government appoints a high level committee to address the problems of the sugar industry," Patel said.
